questions.q: What was the primary condition imposed by the IMF and World Bank on developing countries seeking loans during the 1980s debt crisis?
questions.a: The primary condition was Structural Adjustment Programmes (SAPs) requiring privatisation, trade liberalisation, fiscal austerity, and deregulation. A wrong answer like "they required higher tariffs to protect local industries" reveals the student confuses SAPs with the import-substitution policies of the 1950s-60s that SAPs explicitly dismantled.

questions.q: Why did East Asian economies like South Korea and Taiwan benefit from globalisation while many African nations did not, despite both receiving foreign investment?
questions.a: East Asian states maintained strategic control over capital flows, directed credit to export industries, invested heavily in education, and sequenced liberalisation gradually — unlike African nations forced into rapid, unconditional liberalisation under SAPs that destroyed nascent industries. A wrong answer attributing the difference solely to "culture" or "corruption" misses the critical role of state capacity and policy autonomy.

questions.q: A developing country discovers large oil reserves. An MNC offers to extract it, promising jobs and revenue. The government signs a contract giving the MNC 80% of profits for 30 years with minimal environmental regulation. Using the concept of "unequal exchange," explain why this may deepen underdevelopment.
questions.a: This reflects unequal exchange: the country exports a finite, high-value resource cheaply while importing manufactured goods at high prices, capturing little value-added. The MNC repatriates profits, uses transfer pricing to avoid taxes, and leaves environmental damage. A wrong answer focusing only on "jobs created" ignores the net resource outflow and lost sovereignty over natural wealth.

questions.q: Compare the impact of globalisation on India's pharmaceutical industry (1970s-1990s) versus its textile sector post-1995 WTO Agreement on Textiles and Clothing. What explains the difference?
questions.a: India's 1970 Patent Act allowed process patents only, enabling reverse-engineering of drugs — building a generic pharma giant. Post-1995, textile quotas ended, exposing small powerlooms to Chinese competition without similar state support. The difference: pharma had decades of protected capability-building; textiles faced instant liberalisation. A wrong answer saying "both benefited equally" ignores sector-specific timing and state policy.

questions.q: "Globalisation has reduced global inequality because China and India grew rapidly." Evaluate this claim using the distinction between between-country and within-country inequality.
questions.a: The claim is partially true for between-country inequality (China/India narrowed the gap with the West) but false for within-country inequality (both saw soaring Gini coefficients). Globally, the top 1% captured 27% of growth (1980-2016) while the bottom 50% got 12%. A wrong answer citing only average GDP growth per capita misses the distributional reality that matters for human development.

questions.q: Construct a 4-point argument either defending or criticising the Washington Consensus as a development strategy for a hypothetical mineral-rich, low-industrialised African nation in 1990. Use historical evidence from at least two real countries.
questions.a: A strong critique: (1) Zambia's rapid copper privatisation (1990s) led to tax revenue collapse; (2) Malawi's fertiliser subsidy removal caused famine (2002); (3) Botswana avoided SAPs, used diamond revenue for education/health, achieved upper-middle income; (4) Ethiopia's state-led industrial parks (2010s) created manufacturing jobs without full liberalisation. A poor answer lists only GDP growth figures without structural analysis.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Globalisation's impact on developing countries refers to the uneven economic, social, and political consequences experienced by former colonies and low-income nations from the ______s onward, as they integrated into a world economy shaped by multinational corporations (MNCs), international financial institutions (IMF, World Bank), and trade liberalisation policies, often resulting in growth for some but increased inequality, debt crises, and loss of policy sovereignty for many.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Globalisation's impact on developing countries?
questions.a: Students think "globalisation = free trade benefits everyone equally" and write that developing countries only needed to "open up" to grow.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how structural adjustment programmes (SAPs) altered the economies of at least two developing countries, compare the divergent outcomes for East Asian "tiger economies" versus Sub-Saharan African nations, and evaluate whether globalisation reduced or deepened global inequality using specific evidence.
